explanation: Income tax on individuals, HUFs, firms etc. (non-corporate assessees) is governed by the Income Tax Act, 1961, which remains India's principal direct tax statute.
The CSO's first revised estimate (May 2015) put India's GDP growth for 2014-15 at 7.3% (it was later revised down to 7.2% in January 2016, but 7.3% is the figure this exam-era question intends).
Fiscal policy refers to the government's use of taxation and public expenditure to influence the economy, distinct from monetary policy which deals with money supply and interest rates.

The (now discontinued) budget deficit concept was the gap between total government expenditure and total receipts; among the given options, 'Total receipts – Total expenditures' is the closest match to this definition, though strictly the deficit is expenditure minus receipts.
Minimum Support Price is a government guarantee to farmers to protect them from price crashes and ensure remunerative prices for their produce.
India's GDP growth for Q1 (April-June) FY2019-20, as released by the National Statistical Office, was 5%, the slowest quarterly growth in over six years at that time.
The gilt-edged market is the market for government (and government-guaranteed) securities, so named because such securities are considered safe/risk-free investments.
Barley is a winter (Rabi) crop sown around October-November and harvested in spring; cotton, maize and rice are all Kharif crops.
The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP), under the Ministry of Agriculture, recommends Minimum Support Prices and issue prices to the government.
A balance sheet is a statement of a firm's financial position showing both assets (what it owns) and liabilities (what it owes) as of a given date.
Perspective planning refers to long-term planning, typically spanning 15-25 years, within which shorter Five-Year Plans are framed to achieve incremental targets.

The Rao-Manmohan model refers to the 1991 economic liberalisation reforms initiated under PM P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh, which fell within the 8th Five Year Plan (1992-97).
India's first Industrial Policy Resolution was announced on 6 April 1948, laying down the role of the state and private sector in industrial development.
The Economic Survey is prepared by the Economic Division of the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance, and is tabled in Parliament ahead of the Union Budget.
The Balance of Payments records both the balance of trade (visible current account) and capital receipts and payments (capital account), so it includes both (a) and (b).
The First Five Year Plan (1951-56) was based on the Harrod-Domar growth model, emphasising capital accumulation and agriculture; the Mahalanobis model came in with the Second Plan.
In the 2019 interim budget, Finance Minister Piyush Goyal raised the allocation for North Eastern region infrastructure to Rs. 58,166 crore, a 21% increase over the previous year's budget.

This question circulates widely in Indian competitive-exam banks with 'Both (a) & (b)' as the marked answer: an interim budget is popularly called a mini budget, and in common (if technically loose) usage the term is also used interchangeably with 'vote on account'. Strictly, a vote-on-account covers only the expenditure side while an interim budget is a fuller set of accounts covering both receipts and expenditure, but exam keys for this exact wording treat both labels as applying.

David Malpass became President of the World Bank Group in April 2019 and was serving in that role as of the 2021 exam; Jim Yong Kim was his predecessor and Christine Lagarde headed the IMF, not the World Bank.
The First Five Year Plan was launched in 1951, covering the period 1951-1956, soon after independence.

The First Five Year Plan prioritised agricultural development, including irrigation and food production, to address post-independence food shortages; industrial emphasis came later with the Second Plan.
The Second Five Year Plan (1956-61) was based on the Nehru-Mahalanobis model, which emphasised rapid industrialisation and development of heavy, capital-goods industries.
Mutual Funds in India are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), which frames the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations; AMFI is only an industry association, not a regulator.
The Reserve Bank of India, as the central bank, has the sole authority to issue currency and regulate money supply/circulation in the country.
Commercial banks primarily provide short-term credit for trade, working capital, and consumption needs, unlike industrial/development banks which extend long-term finance.
India's forex reserves comprise four components: Foreign Currency Assets, Gold Reserves, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), and the Reserve Tranche Position in the IMF.
State Bank of India is a Public Sector Bank, with majority ownership held by the Government of India through the Reserve Bank of India / Ministry of Finance.
The Trade (Visible) Account in the Balance of Payments records the export and import of physical/tangible goods, as opposed to invisible items like services, banking charges, or insurance.
The nationalisation of 14 major commercial banks took place on 19 July 1969 under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, aimed at extending credit to priority sectors.
